content:
Ankylosing spondylitis (AS), now often called axial spondyloarthritis, is a long-term inflammatory condition that mainly affects the spine and the joints where the spine meets the pelvis. The classic sign is back pain and stiffness that started before 45, has lasted more than three months, is worse at rest and in the morning, and improves with movement. Daily exercise and medicines can control it well.

Who gets it

AS usually starts in late teens to early 40s. It affects both men and women, although women are often diagnosed later. Many people carry a gene called HLA-B27, but having the gene does not mean you will get AS.

Inflammatory back pain: how it is different

Most back pain is mechanical: it is worse with activity and better with rest. Inflammatory back pain is the opposite:

  • it is worse after rest and in the second half of the night
  • it improves with exercise
  • morning stiffness lasts more than 30 minutes
  • it may wake you in the night
  • there may be pain in the buttocks, sometimes switching sides
  • anti-inflammatory painkillers often help noticeably

Other symptoms

  • pain and swelling in other joints, such as hips, knees or ankles
  • heel pain and pain where tendons attach to bone
  • fatigue
  • uveitis: a painful red eye with blurred vision and light sensitivity. This needs same-day assessment at an eye unit or A&E.
  • links with psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease

Diagnosis

Diagnosis is often delayed because back pain is so common. NICE (NG65) advises GPs to consider referring people with back pain that started before 45 and has lasted over three months to rheumatology if they have features of inflammatory back pain. Tests may include blood tests for inflammation and HLA-B27, and an MRI scan of the pelvis and spine. X-rays may be normal early on.

Treatment

Exercise and physiotherapy. This is central to AS treatment. Daily stretching, posture work, breathing exercises and strengthening help maintain movement. Hydrotherapy can be especially helpful. Many areas run group sessions.

NSAIDs. Anti-inflammatory painkillers are usually the first medicine tried and often work well. Your doctor will check they are safe for you and may add stomach protection.

Biologics and targeted therapies. If NSAIDs do not control symptoms, you may be offered anti-TNF or anti-IL-17 medicines, or a JAK inhibitor, under NICE criteria.

Steroid injections may help a painful joint outside the spine.

Surgery is rarely needed but may include hip replacement if the hip is badly affected.

Living well with AS

  • move every day. Gentle stretches each morning and a longer session several times a week.
  • mind your posture. Sit upright, use a supportive chair and take regular breaks from sitting.
  • stop smoking. It is linked with more severe AS and reduced lung function.
  • sleep on a firm, supportive mattress, with a thin pillow if possible.
  • stay active in sport you enjoy. Swimming is especially good.

Complications to be aware of

Over time, AS can cause the spine to become stiffer and, in some people, bones may fuse. Treatment and exercise reduce this risk. AS also increases the risk of osteoporosis and spinal fractures, which can occur after minor falls. New severe back or neck pain after a fall needs urgent assessment.

Work and support

Many people with AS work full-time. Regular movement breaks, a good chair and desk set-up and flexible hours help. Peer support groups and national charities run exercise sessions and information for people with AS.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • new numbness around your bottom or genitals, problems controlling your bladder or bowels, or new weakness in your legs
  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
